SearchAliases: Zen Zhang Three and Li Four
Senses.Explanation: Zhang Three and Li Four are the records’ stand-in pair for unspecified, readily named people rather than two biographical figures. Baofu Congzhan says that someone passing behind the buddha hall is seen to be Zhang Three or Li Four, then publicly asks why someone passing before it is not seen. Asked “what is the student’s own self?” another answers “Zhang Three and Li Four” (如何是學人自己；張三李四); asked “what is buddha?” another gives the same answer. The Ancestral Hall Collection places their names among distinctions that arise with seeing and hearing: “there are Zhang Three and Li Four, Hu comes and Han goes, the four surnames dwell mixed together” (便有張三李四，胡來漢去，四姓雜居). A later address puts them in the marketplace: “Zhang Three and Li Four sell noisy emptiness; Shide and Hanshan dispute cheap and dear” (張三李四賣囂虛，拾得寒山爭賤貴). Zen bends ordinary stand-in names into recurring answers, visible passersby, and market figures in public addresses; the entry does not decide what any single answer intends.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 既是張公喫酒，因甚李公卻醉？
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lianyue (蓮月禪師語錄). In his own New Year hall address, Lianyue Guangsi repeats Mingjiao's line and asks the assembly why Li is drunk if Zhang drank the wine. Lianyue Guangsi is not yet in the roster; his record supplies the provisional pinyin form.

Senses.Explanation: Mr. Zhang drinks the wine while Mr. Li becomes drunk: the proverb marks a mismatch between actor and consequence. Zhang performs the act of drinking, but Mr. Li bears its effect and gets drunk. The stock line occurs 125 times in 84 allowlisted texts. Masters use that observable mismatch as an answer to otherwise different public questions: why the monastery superintendent lost his eyebrows after Danxia burned the wooden buddha, what Yunmen Wenyan means, and why there is no buddha teaching at the start of a good year. The corpus extends the joke: “Mr. Li sobers up and questions Mr. Zhang, just making Mr. Zhang lose his good temper” (李公醉醒問張公，恰使張公無好氣). In a teaching-seat enumeration it stands beside “Zhong Kui can dance the eighteen beats, the golden cock sings dawn, and the stone woman roams in spring” (鍾馗解舞十八拍，金雞唱曉，石女游春). Lianyue Guangsi turns the mismatch back into a question: “since Mr. Zhang drank the wine, why is Mr. Li drunk?” (既是張公喫酒，因甚李公卻醉). Sixin Wuxin repeats the line, asks its import, and refuses to explain it: “Let the blue sea change as it may; in the end I will not explain it to you” (任從滄海變，終不為君通). Zen bends the comic actor/effect mismatch into a reusable interview answer, verse line, teaching-seat enumeration, and new public question. The records license that structural inference but do not equate the proverb with one universal hidden answer to every case.

Senses.Explanation: The Iron Ox of Shaanfu is a named object in a recurring case, while other iron-ox passages use the durable animal figure without naming that monument. The Shaanfu Iron Ox is the corpus's fixed place-named iron ox, distinct from an unplaced iron-ox figure. Chan masters make it an impossible moving stage-object and public answer. Fenyang Shanzhao answers a question about the student's turning place by saying to water the Shaanfu Iron Ox. Linxi Wenqing's hall address pairs it with the great image of Jiading and makes the two cross their named regions: the image comes through the pass while the Iron Ox enters western Shu. Baiyu Si says that a fire beneath Lake Tai frightens it into running to Silla. These place-name, pairing, watering, and travel predicates establish the recurring named object, but the stored witnesses do not establish what physical object it was or whether it was cast.

Senses.Note: The direct casting witness establishes a cast object locally but does not make every generic iron ox cast, nor does it retroactively identify the Shaanfu Iron Ox's material relation. Fixed longer forms such as the mechanism of an iron ox and the hornless iron ox are retained as family deployments; they do not independently define the bare headword. Mosquito, seal, barrier, and lineage uses are predicates and comparisons, not separate referents.

Senses.Explanation: This separate corpus sense names iron-ox figure, not the Shaanfu Iron Ox. The stored cases keep that referent explicit. An iron-ox figure is an unplaced ox image that Chan masters put into comparisons, mechanism language, and impossible actions. Yaoshan Weiyan compares his former position at Shitou Xiqian to a mosquito on an iron ox. Guishan Lingyou sharpens the physical scene: a mosquito on the iron ox has nowhere to put its mouth. Fengxue Yanzhao compares the patriarchal mind-seal to the mechanism of an iron ox and stages a public exchange over whether to apply the seal. Zhenjing Kewen has a hornless iron ox break an iron barrier, and Yandang Wenji places one in a lineage answer beside the barren woman who bears a child. Baichi Yuan's verse directly speaks of casting an iron ox, establishing a cast object in that occurrence without making casting part of every use. Hongzhi Zhengjue says one tug by the iron ox snaps a gold rope. These are deployments of the generic figure, not the specifically named Shaanfu Iron Ox.

Senses.Explanation: The mechanism of the iron ox is Fengxue Yanzhao's image for the ancestral seal as a working that cannot be handled by choosing motion or rest. His case says that when it goes the seal holds fast, when it stays the seal breaks, and then asks what happens when it neither goes nor stays. Yuanwu Keqin calls this mechanism impossible to cage; later masters quote the case in public interviews and demand an answer beyond merely repeating its terms. The iron ox supplies apparent immovability, while 機 makes that image an active test rather than a static object.

Senses.Explanation: An iron snake cannot bore into it pictures a barrier or closure with no point of entry even for an iron creature built to pierce. Masters use the line as an answer and encounter verdict for what affords no verbal or discriminating purchase; other addresses place it beside a tied sack, an iron wall, or the stock completion that there is nowhere to put down the mouth.

Senses.Explanation: An iron steamed bun looks like food but is too hard to bite, swallow, or eat in the ordinary way. Masters offer it publicly as fare, tell an interlocutor to bite or swallow it, say it blocks the throat, and use it for a case or question that cannot be consumed through easy explanation.
